content: Tetanus is a medical condition characterized by prolonged contraction of skeletal muscle fibers. The primary symptoms are caused by tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic bacterium. Infection typically occurs through wound contamination, often involving a cut or deep puncture wound. As the infection progresses, muscle spasms in the jaw develop, leading to the condition commonly known as lockjaw. This is followed by difficulty swallowing, generalized muscle stiffness, and spasms in other parts of the body. Tetanus specifically affects skeletal muscle, a type of striated muscle. However, cardiac muscle, another type of striated muscle, cannot be tetanized due to its intrinsic electrical properties. In recent years, approximately 11% of reported tetanus cases have been fatal, with the highest mortality rates observed in unvaccinated individuals and those over 60 years of age. Interestingly, C. tetani is recovered from the initial wound in only about 30% of cases and can also be found in individuals who do not have tetanus. The clinical manifestations of tetanus occur when the tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory nerve impulses by interfering with neurotransmitter release, leading to unopposed muscle contraction and spasms. Seizures may occur, and the autonomic nervous system can also be affected. The term tetany refers to sustained muscle contraction but is not synonymous with tetanus. In 1884, Carle and Rattone discovered tetanus by injecting animals with pus from a patient who had died of the disease. In 1924, Descombey developed the tetanus toxoid, which was extensively used during World War II. Tetanus can be classified into four types based on its presentation: neonatal, cephalic, generalized, or local. The causative bacterium, Clostridium tetani, is introduced into the body through a wound. The toxins produced by the bacterium travel via the blood or lymphatic system to target tissues. These toxins act at various sites in the central nervous system, including the spinal cord, peripheral motor end plates, and the brain. They can also affect the sympathetic nervous system. Clostridium tetani is a rod-shaped, anaerobic bacterium that belongs to the genus Clostridium. It is Gram-positive and appears on a Gram stain with a characteristic tennis racket or drumstick shape. The bacterium is found as spores in soil or as parasites in the gastrointestinal tracts of animals. It produces a potent biological toxin, tetanospasmin, which is the causative agent of tetanus. Tetanus must be differentiated from other conditions such as strychnine poisoning, dental infections, drug reactions, hypocalcemia, meningitis, stroke, and stiff person syndrome. Tetanus is an infectious disease that is not contagious and can be prevented with vaccination. In the United States, fewer than 100 cases of tetanus are reported annually, with approximately five deaths attributed to the disease each year. Globally, there are about one million cases of tetanus annually, leading to an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 deaths. The incidence of tetanus in the United States is 0.01 cases per 100,000 individuals. Tetanus is more commonly seen in Hispanics and individuals over the age of 65. The case fatality rate of tetanus is approximately 13.2%. Clostridium tetani spores are found in various environments, including soil, manure, and dust. Individuals in developing countries are at higher risk of acquiring tetanus due to limited access to vaccination and poor hygiene practices. Risk factors for tetanus include contaminated wounds, puncture wounds, crushing injuries, burns, and working in unhygienic environments. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not issued specific guidelines for tetanus screening. The presentation and progression of the disease vary depending on the type of tetanus. Generalized tetanus can involve the respiratory muscles, leading to difficulty breathing. Complications of tetanus include fractures, laryngospasm, aspiration pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. The fatality rate of tetanus is approximately 11%, with prolonged convulsions and contractions contributing to mortality. Tetanus without spasms has an excellent prognosis, and early diagnosis is associated with better outcomes. The history of a patient with tetanus often reveals contamination of a wound with soil, rust-containing metal, or manure. Puncture wounds, burns, animal scratches, fractures, otitis media, and contaminated surgical wounds (e.g., gastrointestinal surgeries or abortions) are common sources. A history of recent injury in a contaminated environment is helpful for diagnosis. Symptoms include trismus (lockjaw), facial muscle spasms (risus sardonicus), neck stiffness, and difficulty swallowing. On physical examination, tetanus may initially present with muscle stiffness, often involving the masseter muscles, accompanied by headache. As the disease progresses, neck stiffness, difficulty swallowing, spasms of various muscle groups (including abdominal muscles), and sweating may occur. Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis, as there are no specific laboratory, imaging, or diagnostic findings associated with the disease. Bacteriologic confirmation is not required, as C. tetani can be found in individuals without tetanus, and only 30% of tetanic wounds yield the pathogen. Tetanus is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization. Treatment includes administration of human tetanus immune globulin (TIG) or equine antitoxin if TIG is unavailable, a tetanus toxoid booster, agents to control muscle spasms, aggressive wound care, and antimicrobial therapy. Mechanical ventilation and agents to manage autonomic nervous system instability may be necessary in severe cases. Surgical intervention, such as wound debridement, is essential for cleaning contaminated wounds. Primary prevention involves vaccination against Clostridium tetani. These individuals typically receive passive immunity with tetanus immune globulin (TIG). The primary cost associated with tetanus is the vaccine. Various trade names and formulations of the tetanus vaccine are available, with costs varying slightly. The DTaP vaccine, which protects against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis, is commonly used.
